title: Why Nobody Can Put Out the Fire Under This Town
description:
In May 1962, the town of Centralia, Pennsylvania, wanted its new dump cleaned up before Memorial Day. The volunteer firemen set it on fire, the way it had been done before. The fire got into the old coal mines underneath the town, and it has been burning ever since.

This is how a dump fire emptied a town of more than 1,000 people: the gas in the basements, the boy who fell into a smoking sinkhole in his grandmother's yard, the buyout, the holdouts who fought the state for 20 years, and the highway that became a tourist attraction.

Facts used: Centralia sits in the anthracite (hard coal) region of eastern Pennsylvania, on top of old mine workings. In May 1962 the borough council had volunteer firemen burn the new landfill in an old strip-mine pit next to the Odd Fellows Cemetery before Memorial Day; the fire was lit around May 27 and put out, then kept coming back. The most accepted account is that it got into the old mines through an unsealed opening in the pit wall; some residents always said it came from an older mine fire from the 1930s. That August, carbon monoxide was found in nearby mines and they were closed. Trenching, flushing and other projects from 1962 to 1978 cost about $3.3 million with limited results. In 1979 mayor John Coddington found the gasoline in his station's underground tank at 172°F. On Feb. 14, 1981, 12-year-old Todd Domboski fell into a steaming sinkhole in his grandmother's yard and held onto tree roots until his cousin Eric pulled him out; the hole was about 150 feet deep with lethal carbon monoxide. A federal study put the cost of digging the fire out at $663 million; residents voted in August 1983 to accept relocation, and Congress provided about $42 million. Pennsylvania took the remaining properties by eminent domain in 1992; Route 61 was closed and rerouted in 1993; the Postal Service retired ZIP code 17927 in 2002. In 2013 the last residents settled with the state: $349,500 and the right to stay for life. The closed stretch of Route 61 became the "Graffiti Highway" and was covered with dirt in 2020. The 2020 census counted 5 people. Estimates say the fire could burn for 250 more years.

The scenes are an animated dramatization.
